title: The New Testament (Tyndale's translation)
alternative_titles: Tyndale's New Testament
The New Testament Translated by William Tyndale
description: William Tyndale's translation of the New Testament from the Greek, the first English New Testament translated directly from the original language and the foundation of all later English Bibles, including the King James Version.
plot_or_argument: A complete translation of the Greek New Testament with prefaces and marginal notes; the Cologne fragment (Matthew 1–22) was interrupted by the authorities in 1525, and the first complete edition appeared at Worms in 1526, followed by Tyndale's thorough revisions of 1534 and 1535.
narrative_structure: Biblical text in the order of the Greek canon, with prologues to the books and expository marginal glosses.
historical_context: Tyndale, denied episcopal support in England (the famous rebuke attributed to a Gloucestershire divine — 'we were better to be without God's law than the Pope's'), went to the continent in 1524; the Cologne printing (Quentel, 1525) was raided, and the Worms octavo of 1526 was smuggled into England, where Bishop Tunstall bought up copies for burning. Tyndale's 1534 revision is the text behind the later English versions.
literary_significance: The fountainhead of English Bible translation: Tyndale's phrasing survives in as much as 80–90 per cent of the King James New Testament, and his English — 'the powers that be', 'a law unto themselves', 'the spirit is willing' — permanently shaped the language's biblical register.
bibliographical_notes: Cologne fragment 1525; first complete edition Worms 1526; revisions Antwerp 1534 and 1535. Standard edition: Tyndale's New Testament, ed. David Daniell (Yale, 1989; modern-spelling ed. 1995).

title: The Pentateuch (Tyndale's translation)
alternative_titles: The Five Books of Moses (Tyndale)
description: Tyndale's translation of the first five books of the Old Testament from the Hebrew, printed at Antwerp in 1530; the first English translation of any part of the Hebrew Bible from the original language.
plot_or_argument: A complete translation of Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, with prefaces to each book explaining its sense and typological bearing, and a prologue to the whole ('W. T. to the Reader') setting out Tyndale's principles of translation from the Hebrew.
narrative_structure: Biblical text in the Hebrew order, with per-book prefaces and glosses; Genesis and Numbers were printed separately with their own title pages.
historical_context: Tyndale learned Hebrew on the continent (probably from Jewish scholars), and the Pentateuch of 1530 was printed by Hans Luft at Antwerp (or Marburg) and smuggled into England; it supplied the Old Testament basis for the Matthew Bible (1537) and, through it, for the Great Bible and the King James Version.
literary_significance: The first English translation from the Hebrew and the origin of the English Old Testament's distinctive phrasing ('let there be light', 'the Lord bless thee and keep thee'); it established the principle that the Bible must be rendered from the original tongues.
bibliographical_notes: First edition Antwerp 1530 (STC 2350); standard edition: Tyndale's Old Testament, ed. David Daniell (Yale, 1992).

title: The Obedience of a Christian Man
alternative_titles: The Obedience of a Christen Man and How Christen Rulers Ought to Governe
description: Tyndale's treatise on the obedience owed by Christians to rulers and on the reading of scripture, printed at Antwerp in 1528; the book that, shown to Henry VIII, drew the king's reported remark that 'this is the book for me and all kings to read'.
plot_or_argument: The book argues that every Christian — ploughman, weaver, or king — must obey his temporal rulers, whom God has ordained; it attacks the pope's claim to absolve subjects of allegiance, defends vernacular scripture against the charge that it breeds heresy, and expounds the duties of fathers, husbands, masters, and kings from the New Testament.
narrative_structure: A continuous treatise divided into topical sections on the estates and their duties, with a famous preface on the reading of scripture.
historical_context: Printed at Antwerp in 1528 (by Hans Luft's press or its associates); Anne Boleyn's copy reached Henry VIII, and the book's doctrine of royal supremacy over the church made it a cornerstone of Henrician propaganda, feeding directly into the Reformation statutes of the 1530s.
literary_significance: The most politically consequential English book of the early Reformation: its doctrine of obedience made the English Reformation conceivable as an act of state, and its defence of vernacular scripture became the platform of the English Bible.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1528 (STC 24446); modern edition: The Obedience of a Christian Man, ed. David Daniell (Penguin, 2000).

title: The Parable of the Wicked Mammon
alternative_titles: The Parable of the Wycked Mammon
description: Tyndale's exposition of the parable of the unjust steward (Luke 16), printed in 1528; his first published work and the classic statement of the Reformation doctrine of justification by faith alone.
plot_or_argument: The treatise expounds the parable to teach that works do not justify but follow justification: the faithful are justified by faith in Christ's blood, and good works are the fruit of that faith, performed to one's neighbour without thought of merit; Tyndale defends the doctrine against the charge of encouraging licence and attacks the theology of merits, purgatory, and the intercession of saints.
narrative_structure: A continuous doctrinal exposition with a preface 'To the Reader', arguing from scripture in Tyndale's plainest homiletic style.
historical_context: Printed in 1528 (STC 24454), the year of the Obedience, during Tyndale's exile in the Low Countries; it was among the first English books to state the Lutheran doctrine of justification, and it made Tyndale the prime target of More's Dialogue Concerning Heresies.
literary_significance: The first full English statement of justification by faith and the opening salvo of the English print war between Tyndale and More; its doctrine and its plain style set the terms of the English Reformation debate.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1528 (STC 24454); modern edition: in The Works of William Tyndale, ed. Henry Walter (Parker Society, 1848), and Doctrinal Treatises, ed. Henry Walter (Parker Society, 1848).

title: The Practice of Prelates
alternative_titles: The Practyse of Prelates
description: Tyndale's polemic against the English bishops and Cardinal Wolsey, published in 1530, arguing that the prelates' craft had corrupted both church and state and broken the king's marriage.
plot_or_argument: The book traces the 'practice' (craft) of the prelates through English history, attacks Wolsey's legatine power and the annulment proceedings, defends the king's cause against the pope's usurped jurisdiction, and argues from scripture that no man may set himself over kings; it closes with the charge that the bishops oppose the vernacular scripture because it exposes their greed.
narrative_structure: A continuous polemic in three movements — historical narrative, political argument, and scriptural proof — addressed to the king, lords, and commons.
historical_context: Published in 1530 at the height of the king's 'great matter', while Wolsey's fall was fresh (November 1529); Tyndale's attack on the annulment as the prelates' contrivance, and his denial of the pope's dispensing power, aligned him with the Henrician propaganda campaign while going further than the king would allow.
literary_significance: The most aggressive of Tyndale's political works and a landmark in the English tradition of anti-prelatical polemic that runs to Milton; it documents the convergence of Reformation doctrine and Tudor statecraft.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1530 (STC 24465); modern edition: in The Works of William Tyndale, ed. Henry Walter (Parker Society, 1849).

title: An Answer unto Sir Thomas More's Dialogue
alternative_titles: An Answere unto Sir Thomas Mores Dialoge
description: Tyndale's reply to More's Dialogue Concerning Heresies, published in 1531; the central exchange of the great English print war between the two men.
plot_or_argument: The book answers More point by point: Tyndale defends his translation of the New Testament against More's charges of corruption, argues that the church is the congregation of believers known by scripture, not the pope's institution, denies that he teaches rebellion, and attacks More's church of ceremonies with the full battery of scriptural citation, closing with a devastating personal address to 'Master More'.
narrative_structure: A point-by-point refutation following the order of More's Dialogue, in Tyndale's plain and urgent prose; the first major English controversy conducted wholly in print.
historical_context: Published in 1531 as the direct reply to More's Dialogue Concerning Heresies (1529); More answered with the Confutation of Tyndale's Answer (1532–33), completing the most sustained intellectual duel of the English Reformation, conducted from exile and the chancellorship respectively.
literary_significance: One half of the greatest controversy in early English prose: the Tyndale–More exchange fixed the rhetorical terms of the Reformation debate, and the Answer remains the fullest statement of Tyndale's ecclesiology and translation theory.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1531 (STC 24437); modern edition: An Answer unto Sir Thomas Mores Dialoge, ed. Anne M. O'Donnell and Jared Wicks (Catholic University of America Press, 2000).

title: The Book of Common Prayer (1549)
alternative_titles: The First Prayer Book of Edward VI
The Booke of the Common Prayer and Administracion of the Sacramentes
description: The first Book of Common Prayer, compiled chiefly by Thomas Cranmer and imposed by the Act of Uniformity of 1549 as the single liturgy of the English church; the foundational text of Anglican worship.
plot_or_argument: The book replaces the medieval service books (missal, breviary, manual, pontifical) with one English liturgy: Morning and Evening Prayer, the collects, the order for Holy Communion, baptism, confirmation, matrimony, visitation of the sick, burial, and the ordination rites, with the psalter and lectionary — retaining much medieval devotion while recasting the eucharist as a communion of all the people in both kinds.
narrative_structure: A complete liturgical manual arranged by rite, with rubrics, calendar, and lectionary; the prose is Cranmer's — sonorous, cadenced, and scriptural.
historical_context: Drafted in 1548–49 by Cranmer with a committee of bishops and divines, authorized by the first Act of Uniformity (January 1549), and introduced at Whitsun 1549, provoking the Prayer Book Rebellion in Devon and Cornwall; the book was revised in 1552 (the Second Prayer Book), restored by Elizabeth in 1559, and its language survives in the 1662 book used for four centuries.
literary_significance: The greatest single achievement of English liturgical prose: Cranmer's collects ('whose service is perfect freedom', 'read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest') entered the language itself, and the book's cadences shaped English prose from Hooker to the Authorized Version and beyond.
attribution_notes: The book is the work of Cranmer and his committee; the title page names no author, and the record attributes the compilation to Cranmer as chief author, following universal scholarly usage.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1549 (STC 16267–16277, various printings); standard edition: The Book of Common Prayer: The Texts of 1549, 1559, and 1662, ed. Brian Cummings (Oxford, 2011).

title: The Book of Homilies
alternative_titles: Certain Sermons or Homilies Appointed by the King's Majesty to Be Declared and Read
description: The first official book of sermons of the Church of England, issued in 1547 under the direction of Thomas Cranmer (who wrote several of the homilies himself) to be read in parish churches; a principal vehicle of Reformation doctrine for the laity.
plot_or_argument: Twelve homilies expound the Protestant faith in plain English: on scripture, the misery of mankind, salvation by faith alone, good works, Christian love, against swearing and perjury, against strife, obedience to rulers, and against whoredom and adultery — each designed to be read from the pulpit by clergy who could not preach.
narrative_structure: Twelve self-contained sermons, each with a scriptural text, exposition, and application, written for oral delivery by non-preaching clergy.
historical_context: Issued in 1547, the first year of Edward VI, as part of the royal Injunctions requiring the homilies' use; the homily 'Of Good Works' and others are Cranmer's own, and the second book (with the famous homily 'Against Disobedience and Wilful Rebellion') followed in 1571, making the two books the official theology of the Elizabethan church.
literary_significance: The official voice of the English Reformation for ordinary congregations: the homilies translated Protestant doctrine into a national plain style and remained binding on the church for three centuries, feeding directly into the religious language of the Elizabethans.
attribution_notes: The book is a collaborative production of Cranmer, Thomas Becon, and other reformers; the record attributes it to Cranmer as the supervising compiler, following standard scholarship, while noting the collaboration.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1547 (STC 13638.5 et seq.); standard edition: Certain Sermons or Homilies (1547) and A Homily against Disobedience and Wilful Rebellion (1570), ed. Ronald B. Bond (Toronto, 1987); also in The Homilies, ed. Ian Lancashire (Toronto, forthcoming/online).

title: A Defence of the True and Catholic Doctrine of the Sacrament
alternative_titles: The Defence of the True and Catholike Doctrine of the Sacrament of the Body and Bloud of Our Saviour Christ
description: Cranmer's principal theological work, published in 1550, defining the eucharist against both transubstantiation and mere memorialism; the fullest statement of the Reformed doctrine of the sacrament in English.
plot_or_argument: The book argues from scripture and the fathers that Christ is truly but spiritually present in the eucharist, received by faith; it refutes the Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation (against Stephen Gardiner) and the Zwinglian reduction of the sacrament to a bare sign, distinguishing 'sacramentally' from 'corporally', and it defends the vernacular liturgy and communion in both kinds.
narrative_structure: Five books of doctrinal argument with patristic citation, cast as a reply to Gardiner's defence of the corporal presence.
historical_context: Published in 1550 during Cranmer's ascendancy under Edward VI, in the controversy with Bishop Stephen Gardiner (imprisoned for his opposition); the doctrine of the Defence shaped the communion rite of the 1552 Prayer Book, and Cranmer recanted it under Mary before renouncing his recantations at the stake in 1556.
literary_significance: The classic English statement of the Reformed eucharist and Cranmer's most sustained piece of theological prose; it fixed the middle course of Anglican sacramental doctrine for centuries.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1550 (STC 6000); modern edition: The Work of Thomas Cranmer, ed. G. E. Duffield (1964); standard study: Diarmaid MacCulloch, Thomas Cranmer: A Life (Yale, 1996).

title: Sermon of the Plough
alternative_titles: Sermon on the Ploughers
The Plough Sermon
description: Hugh Latimer's most famous sermon, preached at Paul's Cross on 18 January 1548 and printed the same year; the classic Protestant sermon of social criticism, built on the text of the sower.
plot_or_argument: Taking the gospel of the sower, Latimer expounds the 'plough' of preaching, the 'seed' of God's word, and the spiritual husbandry required of clergy and laity alike; he attacks the idleness of prelates ('unpreaching prelates'), the rack-renting of landlords, and the neglect of the poor, calling the realm to the work of the spiritual plough — a sustained sermon of estates satire turned to gospel ends.
narrative_structure: A single sermon structured by the parable's allegory — the plough, the seed, the soil — with digressions into the abuses of church and commonwealth.
historical_context: Preached at Paul's Cross on 18 January 1548, in the first months of Edward VI's reign, as part of the reform campaign against images and non-residence; printed by John Day in 1548 and reprinted through the century, the sermon made Latimer the voice of the Edwardian Reformation's social conscience.
literary_significance: The most celebrated English sermon of the Reformation: its homely agricultural allegory and its fearless attack on clerical and landlord abuses made it the model of the Protestant pulpit's social criticism from the sixteenth century to the nineteenth.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1548 (STC 15276); modern edition: Sermons by Hugh Latimer, ed. G. E. Corrie (Parker Society, 1844); also in Sermons and Remains of Hugh Latimer, ed. G. E. Corrie (Parker Society, 1845).

title: The Sermons before King Edward VI
alternative_titles: The Seven Sermons before Edward VI
Latimer's Lenten Sermons of 1549
description: Hugh Latimer's seven Lenten sermons preached before King Edward VI in the privy garden at Westminster in 1549 and printed the same year; the fullest surviving example of Latimer's court preaching.
plot_or_argument: Preached weekly in Lent 1549, the sermons press the young king and his court with the duties of the magistrate: Latimer denounces the greed of landlords and enclosers, the plunder of church goods, the oppression of the poor, and the corruption of officials, urging the king to be the father of the commonwealth and warning that England's plagues are God's judgement on its sins.
narrative_structure: Seven self-contained sermons, each on a set text, in Latimer's direct, colloquial, and anecdotal style, with running rebukes of his courtly audience.
historical_context: Preached at Westminster in Lent 1549, the year of the First Prayer Book, the rebellions of 1549, and the fall of Protector Somerset; printed by John Day in 1549, the sermons document the preaching office at the summit of the state and the social crisis of the mid-Tudor years.
literary_significance: The classic example of court preaching in English and a prime source for the social history of Edwardian England; Latimer's plainspoken rebukes of the powerful made him the archetype of the prophetic preacher.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1549 (STC 15274); modern edition: Sermons by Hugh Latimer, ed. G. E. Corrie (Parker Society, 1844).

title: The Coverdale Bible
alternative_titles: Biblia: The Bible Faithfully Translated into English
description: Miles Coverdale's translation of the whole Bible into English, printed in 1535 (probably at Antwerp); the first complete printed Bible in English.
plot_or_argument: A complete Bible — Old Testament, Apocrypha, and New Testament — translated 'out of Douche and Latyn' (German and Latin versions) as Coverdale's title page honestly states, with Tyndale's New Testament and Pentateuch incorporated; dedicated to Henry VIII, with a preface defending vernacular scripture.
narrative_structure: The full biblical canon with prologues, chapter summaries, and a dedication to the king.
historical_context: Printed in 1535, probably at Antwerp (the colophon of some copies points to Cologne); Anne Boleyn's patronage and Cromwell's diplomacy won it royal acceptance, and in 1537 it was licensed for sale in England, making the English Bible legal for the first time.
literary_significance: The first complete English Bible in print and the bridge from Tyndale to the authorized versions: its psalter became the Prayer Book psalter of 1662, still sung in Anglican worship, and its title page initiated the tradition of the English Bible as a national book.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1535 (STC 2063); standard edition: The Coverdale Bible (1535), with a modern-spelling edition of the Psalter in The Book of Common Prayer, ed. Brian Cummings (Oxford, 2011); facsimile: Scolar Press, 1975.

title: The Great Bible
alternative_titles: The Byble in Englyshe
Cromwell's Bible
Cranmer's Bible
description: The first authorized English Bible, a revision of Matthew's Bible (itself based on Tyndale and Coverdale) carried out by Miles Coverdale and printed in Paris and London in 1539 under Thomas Cromwell's patronage; the Bible ordered to be set up in every parish church.
plot_or_argument: A complete Bible in large folio format, with the title page by Hans Holbein showing Henry VIII handing the Word to Cranmer and Cromwell; the text revises the Matthew Bible's Old Testament against the Hebrew and Latin, and its 1540 second edition carried Cranmer's preface, giving the book its later name.
narrative_structure: The full biblical canon with prologues, summaries, and the famous illustrated title page.
historical_context: Commissioned by Cromwell and begun in Paris (the French printing was seized by the Inquisition, and the presses moved to London), the Great Bible of 1539 was ordered by the injunctions of 1538 to be placed in every parish church; its psalter entered the Prayer Book tradition, and it remained the standard English Bible until the Bishops' Bible of 1568.
literary_significance: The Bible that made the English Bible a public institution: chained in the churches, read aloud to the people, it established the vernacular scriptures at the centre of English religious life and supplied the psalter of the Prayer Book.
attribution_notes: The revision is Coverdale's, on the basis of the Matthew Bible (edited by John Rogers from Tyndale and Coverdale); the record attributes the work to Coverdale as revising editor, following standard usage.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1539 (STC 2068); second edition with Cranmer's preface 1540 (STC 2069); standard study: David Daniell, The Bible in English (Yale, 2003).

title: Goostly Psalmes and Spirituall Songes
alternative_titles: Ghostly Psalms and Spiritual Songs
description: Miles Coverdale's collection of metrical psalms, hymns, and carols translated from the German (chiefly Luther), printed c. 1535; the first English hymn book, intended for congregational singing.
plot_or_argument: Forty-one pieces — metrical versions of the psalms, Luther's hymns (including 'Ein feste Burg' as 'Our God is a defence and tower'), the Creed, the Lord's Prayer, and canticles — each with its tune indicated, prefaced by an epistle on the right use of psalmody in church and home.
narrative_structure: A hymn book arranged by liturgical use, with a preface on singing and notes of the tunes to which the pieces are set.
meter_and_prosody: Metrical stanzas in ballad and hymn metres, set to German tunes
historical_context: Printed c. 1535 during Coverdale's continental exile, drawing on the Wittenberg hymn books; Henry VIII's 1546 proclamation against 'ballads, rhymes, and lewd songs' included it among the books to be burned, and only one complete copy survives (Queen's College, Oxford).
literary_significance: The first English hymn book and the beginning of English congregational song; its psalms anticipate the metrical psalters of Sternhold and Hopkins, and its translation of 'Ein feste Burg' entered the English hymnic tradition.
bibliographical_notes: Printed c. 1535 (STC 5892, unique complete copy); modern edition: Remains of Myles Coverdale, ed. George Pearson (Parker Society, 1846); facsimile in The Ghostly Psalms and Spiritual Songs of Miles Coverdale, ed. Robin A. Leaver (1999).

title: The Examinations of Anne Askew
alternative_titles: The First Examination of Anne Askew
The Latter Examination of Anne Askew
description: Anne Askew's first-person accounts of her two examinations for heresy before the ecclesiastical authorities, printed in 1546 and 1547 with prefaces by John Bale; the most important English text written by a woman in the first half of the sixteenth century.
plot_or_argument: Askew narrates her arrest and first examination before the bishop's chancellor (March 1545) and the second, harsher examination before Bishop Bonner, Bishop Gardiner, Wriothesley, and the privy council (1545–46), recording her scriptural answers on the eucharist, her refusal to name her fellow evangelicals, and her racking in the Tower — 'I answered that I would not deny my master and my God'; the account ends with her condemnation, the burning following on 16 July 1546.
narrative_structure: A first-person testimonial narrative in two parts, with Bale's framing prefaces and his 'elucidations' printed alongside; the latter examination includes the exchange with the council and the account of the rack.
principal_characters: Anne Askew (narrator); Bishop Edmund Bonner; Bishop Stephen Gardiner; Thomas Wriothesley; Christopher Dare; John Bale (editor)
historical_context: Written in prison in 1545–46, smuggled out, and printed by Bale at Wesel in 1546 (first examination) and 1547 (latter examination) as Protestant propaganda against the Henrician church; John Foxe incorporated the Examinations into the Book of Martyrs, making Askew the most famous of the Henrician women martyrs.
literary_significance: The first sustained autobiographical narrative by an English woman in print and the founding text of the English martyr tradition; Askew's scriptural self-defence under torture made her a model of the speaking female subject for later centuries.
attribution_notes: The text is Askew's own account, edited (and heavily framed) by John Bale; the record attributes authorship to Askew, with Bale's role as editor noted.
bibliographical_notes: First examination printed Wesel 1546 (STC 848); latter examination 1547 (STC 850); standard edition: The Examinations of Anne Askew, ed. Elaine V. Beilin (Oxford, 1996).

title: Prayers or Meditations
alternative_titles: Prayers Stirring the Mind unto Heavenly Meditations
description: Catherine Parr's book of devotional prayers and meditations, published in 1545; the first book published by an English queen under her own name, which ran through nineteen editions by 1600.
plot_or_argument: The book adapts the third book of Thomas à Kempis's Imitation of Christ into a sequence of prayers, meditations on the passion, and exhortations to penitence, faith, and the amendment of life, addressed to the reader in the queen's own voice as a fellow sinner seeking grace.
narrative_structure: A devotional manual of prayers and meditations arranged by spiritual states — contrition, faith, thanksgiving — with scriptural centos and personal application.
historical_context: Published in 1545 by Thomas Berthelet with the queen's name on the title page, in the months when Parr's evangelical household (including Askew's associates) was under suspicion; the book's success established the royal devotional voice that Elizabeth I and others would imitate.
literary_significance: The first printed book by an English queen and a landmark in the history of women's devotional writing; its combination of à Kempis's piety with Reformation emphasis on faith made it the century's most popular royal book.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1545 (STC 4818); modern edition: Katherine Parr: Complete Works and Correspondence, ed. Janel Mueller (Chicago, 2011).

title: The Lamentation of a Sinner
alternative_titles: The Lamentacion of a Synner
description: Catherine Parr's spiritual autobiography and treatise on justification by faith, published posthumously in 1547; the fullest statement of the queen's evangelical faith.
plot_or_argument: Parr confesses her former life 'in superstition and ignorance', recounts her awakening to the doctrine of justification by faith through the reading of scripture, and expounds the gospel of free grace against the reliance on works, ending with a meditation on the passion and an exhortation to trust wholly in Christ's merits.
narrative_structure: A two-part work: a first-person confession and conversion narrative, followed by a doctrinal exposition of faith, grace, and the law.
historical_context: Written in the last years of Henry VIII's reign, when Parr's evangelical circle faced persecution (Askew was burned in July 1546), and published by William Cecil (later Lord Burghley) in 1547 after the king's death; the book became a manual of Edwardian Protestant piety.
literary_significance: The first spiritual autobiography by an English queen and an important document of the Reformation's inward turn; it shows the queen — the only woman whose books were printed in her lifetime in Tudor England — articulating the doctrine of faith in her own voice.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1547 (STC 4827); modern edition: Katherine Parr: Complete Works and Correspondence, ed. Janel Mueller (Chicago, 2011).

title: King Johan
alternative_titles: Kynge Johan
description: John Bale's historical morality play of King John, composed c. 1538 and surviving in a single manuscript revised in the 1550s; regarded as the first English history play.
plot_or_argument: King John, the champion of England's ancient liberties against the papal usurpation, is beset by the allegorical forces of Rome — Sedition, Dissimulation, Usurped Power, Private Wealth — and the clergy, who stir rebellion and bring about his poisoning by Dissimulation disguised as a monk; Widow England and her allies Verity and Imperial Majesty restore the true succession, and the play ends with John vindicated as a proto-Protestant martyr and the papal power expelled.
narrative_structure: A two-part play mixing historical persons (John, Stephen Langton, the Pope) with morality personifications, revised by Bale to address Elizabeth I; the structure alternates the king's historical action with the Vices' comic plotting.
principal_characters: King John; Widow England; Sedition; Dissimulation; Usurped Power; Private Wealth; Verity; Imperial Majesty; Nobility; Clergy; Civil Order; Stephen Langton; Pope Innocent III
historical_context: Composed c. 1538 during Bale's Protestant exile/activity under Cromwell's patronage, at the moment when Henry VIII's break with Rome made King John a usable hero; Bale revised the play for Elizabeth (the manuscript addresses her), aligning it with the Elizabethan settlement's anti-papal politics.
literary_significance: The first English history play: its fusion of the morality tradition with national history and its anti-papal reading of King John set the pattern for the Elizabethan history play, directly anticipating Shakespeare's King John.
bibliographical_notes: Unique manuscript (Huntington Library, MS HM 3), first printed by the Camden Society in 1838; standard edition: The Complete Plays of John Bale, vol. 1, ed. Peter Happé (Brewer, 1985).

title: The Chief Promises of God unto Man
alternative_titles: God's Promises
A Tragedy or Interlude Manifesting the Chief Promises of God unto Man
description: John Bale's interlude of the covenants of God from Adam to Christ, composed c. 1538 and printed at Wesel in 1547; a dramatic sermon on the promises fulfilled in the gospel.
plot_or_argument: God the Father, in seven acts, makes his successive promises to man — to Adam of the woman's seed, to Noah of the rainbow covenant, to Abraham of the blessing of nations, to Moses of the law, to David of the everlasting throne, to Isaiah of the virgin's son, and to John the Baptist of the Lamb of God — each act closing with a prayer or antiphon, the whole demonstrating that the Old Testament is fulfilled in Christ.
narrative_structure: Seven acts, each a dialogue between God the Father (as Pater Coelestis) and a biblical figure, framed by a prologue (Bale as Prolocutor) and an epilogue; the play is a doctrinal pageant of the covenants.
principal_characters: God the Father (Pater Coelestis); Adam; Noah; Abraham; Moses; David; Isaiah; John the Baptist; Baleus Prolocutor
meter_and_prosody: Couplets and stanzaic passages with antiphons
historical_context: Written c. 1538 during Bale's service as a Protestant dramatist under Cromwell, and printed at Wesel in 1547 in the collection of Bale's biblical plays; the play embodies the Protestant programme of replacing the old mysteries with doctrinal drama drawn from scripture alone.
literary_significance: The most accomplished of Bale's biblical interludes and a model of Reformation dramaturgy: its covenant structure turned the mystery-cycle tradition to doctrinal ends and influenced the biblical drama of the Elizabethan church.
bibliographical_notes: First printed Wesel 1547 (STC 1305); standard edition: The Complete Plays of John Bale, vol. 2, ed. Peter Happé (Brewer, 1986).
